module.title: Dining Out: Ordering Food & Drinks
module.objective: Order food and drinks politely in a café or restaurant using polite requests like 'I would like' and 'Could I have'.

subModules.title: Reading Mission: A Meal at the Café
subModules.grammarFocus: Polite requests with 'I would like' (I'd like) and 'Could I have'
subModules.vocabularyFocus: Restaurant and café vocabulary: food items, drinks, polite phrases for ordering

content.summary: Welcome to your Reading Mission! In this lesson, you will read a short conversation that takes place in a café. Two friends, Tom and Lisa, visit a café and order food and drinks from a waiter. As you read, you will see how they use polite phrases like 'I would like' and 'Could I have' to order. You will also learn important restaurant vocabulary and practice understanding the main idea and key details of a simple dialogue. By the end of this mission, you will feel more confident reading and understanding real restaurant conversations in English. Let's get started!

linguisticTarget.grammar: Polite request structures: 'I would like + a/an/some + noun' and 'Could I have + a/an/some + noun + please?' Also practice the contraction 'I'd like' as a natural spoken form of 'I would like'.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Restaurant and café words including menu, order, sandwich, bill, table, drink, water, coffee, dessert, ready, waiter, salad, juice, and check.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Skimming the passage first to understand the general situation (Who? Where? What?), then scanning for specific details such as what each person orders and how they ask politely.

learningObjectives: Understand the main idea of a short A1 conversation set in a café or restaurant.
Identify key details including what food and drinks each person orders.
Recognize polite ordering patterns: 'I would like...', 'I'd like...', and 'Could I have...?' in context.
Distinguish between polite and impolite ways of ordering in English.
Build confidence with essential restaurant vocabulary through reading practice.

contextWarmup.prompt: You are at a café and the waiter asks: 'What would you like to drink?' Which is the MOST polite answer?
options: I'd like some orange juice, please.
contextWarmup.explanation: Great job if you chose the first option! 'I'd like some orange juice, please' is the most polite way to order a drink. It uses the contraction 'I'd like' (short for 'I would like') and adds 'please' at the end. The other options sound too direct or even rude in a restaurant setting.

rules: Use 'I would like' or 'I'd like' followed by a/an/some + item to order politely. Example: 'I'd like a chicken sandwich, please.' This is much more polite than saying 'I want a chicken sandwich.'
Use 'Could I have' + a/an/some + item + please? to make a very polite request. Example: 'Could I have some water, please?' Remember: 'Could I have' is a question, so it ends with a question mark.
Always add 'please' at the end of your order to sound friendly and respectful. Compare: 'I'd like a coffee' (okay) vs. 'I'd like a coffee, please' (better and more polite!).

Use 'a' before singular countable nouns starting with a consonant sound (a sandwich, a table), 'an' before vowel sounds (an orange juice), and 'some' before uncountable nouns or plural items (some water, some fries).
When you finish your meal, you can say 'Could I have the bill, please?' or 'Could I have the check, please?' to ask the waiter for the payment.

commonTrap.explanation: Many beginners mix up the two polite patterns. They write 'Could I like a sandwich?' or 'I would have a sandwich?' — but these are incorrect combinations! Remember: 'Could I HAVE' and 'I would LIKE' are two separate fixed patterns. Do not mix the verbs between them.
commonTrap.wrong: Could I like a chicken sandwich, please?
commonTrap.correct: Could I have a chicken sandwich, please? OR I would like a chicken sandwich, please.

sections.title: Reading Passage: Lunch at Sunny Café

content.context: Tom and Lisa are friends. They go to the Sunny Café for lunch on a Saturday afternoon. A friendly waiter helps them with their order.
content.text:
Tom and Lisa walk into the Sunny Café. A waiter smiles and says, "Good afternoon! A table for two?" Lisa says, "Yes, please." The waiter shows them a nice table near the window.

The waiter gives them the menu. After a few minutes, he comes back. "Are you ready to order?" he asks.

Tom says, "Yes, I'd like a chicken sandwich and some orange juice, please." Lisa says, "Could I have a green salad, please? And I'd like a coffee with milk."

The waiter writes everything down. "Great choices! Would you like any dessert today?" Tom answers, "Not right now, thank you."

After they finish eating, Lisa says to the waiter, "Could I have the bill, please?" The waiter brings the bill. Tom says, "The food is delicious! Thank you very much." The waiter smiles and says, "You're welcome! Have a nice day!"

highlights.note: This is the contraction of 'I would like' — a polite way to say what you want to order.
A very polite question pattern used to request something. Always followed by a noun.
Adding 'please' makes any request sound more polite and friendly.
A common café food item. Notice 'a' before the singular noun.
A salad made with fresh green vegetables. A healthy lunch choice!
The paper that shows how much money you need to pay at a restaurant.
The waiter uses this polite question to offer something to customers.
A popular drink. Notice 'some' is used before uncountable drink nouns: 'some orange juice'.

gistQuestion.prompt: What is this passage mainly about?
options: Two friends ordering food and drinks politely at a café.
A waiter cooking food in the kitchen.
Two friends shopping at a supermarket.
gistQuestion.explanation: The passage is about Tom and Lisa visiting the Sunny Café and ordering their lunch politely using phrases like 'I'd like' and 'Could I have'. The whole conversation happens between the two friends and their waiter.

detailQuestions.prompt: What does Tom order to eat?
detailQuestions.explanation: Tom says, 'I'd like a chicken sandwich and some orange juice, please.' So his food order is a chicken sandwich. The green salad is what Lisa orders.

detailQuestions.prompt: What does Lisa order to drink?
detailQuestions.explanation: Lisa says, 'I'd like a coffee with milk.' Tom is the one who orders orange juice, not Lisa.

detailQuestions.prompt: How does Lisa ask for the bill at the end?
options: Could I have the bill, please?
detailQuestions.explanation: Lisa uses the polite pattern 'Could I have the bill, please?' This is the correct and polite way to ask for the bill in a restaurant, just as we learned in this unit.

options: No, he says 'Not right now, thank you.'
detailQuestions.explanation: When the waiter asks 'Would you like any dessert today?', Tom answers 'Not right now, thank you.' This means he does not want dessert at this time.

questions.question: In the passage, where do Tom and Lisa sit?
options: At a table near the window.
At a table near the door.
questions.answer: At a table near the window.
questions.explanation: The passage says, 'The waiter shows them a nice table near the window.' So they sit near the window.

questions.question: Which polite phrase does Tom use to order his food?
questions.explanation: Tom says, 'I'd like a chicken sandwich and some orange juice, please.' He uses the polite contraction 'I'd like' which is short for 'I would like'. He does NOT say 'I want' or 'Give me'.

questions.question: Which polite phrase does Lisa use to order her salad?
options: Could I have a green salad, please?
questions.answer: Could I have a green salad, please?
questions.explanation: Lisa says, 'Could I have a green salad, please?' She uses the polite request pattern 'Could I have + item + please?' This is one of the two key polite patterns in this unit.

questions.question: What does the waiter say at the very end of the conversation?
options: You're welcome! Have a nice day!
questions.answer: You're welcome! Have a nice day!
questions.explanation: The last line of the passage is the waiter saying, 'You're welcome! Have a nice day!' This is a friendly and common way for waiters to say goodbye to customers.

questions.question: Read this sentence: 'Could I have some water, please?' What type of sentence is this?
questions.explanation: 'Could I have some water, please?' uses the polite pattern 'Could I have...?' plus 'please'. This makes it a polite request — not a command. Commands sound like 'Give me water!' which is not polite.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'I would like' to order a drink?
options: I would like some orange juice, please.
I would like ordering some orange juice.
I would have some orange juice, please.
questions.answer: I would like some orange juice, please.
questions.explanation: The correct pattern is 'I would like + a/an/some + noun'. You should NOT add '-ing' after 'would like' when ordering a specific item. Also, 'I would have' is not the standard polite ordering pattern — the correct form is 'I would like' or 'Could I have'.

questions.question: In the passage, who asks for the bill — Tom or Lisa?
options: The waiter brings the bill without anyone asking.
questions.explanation: The passage clearly states: 'Lisa says to the waiter, "Could I have the bill, please?"' So it is Lisa who politely requests the bill.

questions.question: What does Tom say about the food?
questions.explanation: Near the end of the passage, Tom says, 'The food is delicious! Thank you very much.' He is happy with the food and thanks the waiter.

subModules.title: Listening Mission: Catching Orders at the Café

content.summary: In this listening mission, you will hear a conversation at a café. Two customers, Sarah and Tom, are ordering food and drinks from a waiter. Pay close attention to the polite phrases they use to make their orders. At A1 level, the most important phrases for ordering are 'I would like…' and 'Could I have…?' followed by the name of the food or drink. Listen for these key patterns, and also notice how the waiter asks questions and confirms the order. Focus on the names of food items, drinks, and polite words like 'please' and 'thank you'.
learningObjectives: Identify polite ordering phrases such as 'I would like' and 'Could I have' in spoken English.
Recognise common food and drink vocabulary when spoken at natural A1-level speed.
Understand a waiter's questions about orders, such as 'What would you like to drink?' and 'Are you ready to order?'
Notice the use of 'please' and 'thank you' in a restaurant conversation.

keyPhrases.note: A polite way to say what you want to order. It is more formal than 'I want'. Often followed by a food or drink item.
A very polite question form used to request something. Common in restaurants and cafés when ordering.
A standard question that a waiter asks when they come to your table. You can answer 'Yes' or 'Not yet'.

keyPhrases.phrase: What would you like to drink?
keyPhrases.note: The waiter uses this question to ask about your drink choice. Listen for 'drink' as the key word.
A short phrase the waiter uses to ask the next person at the table for their order.

keyPhrases.phrase: Your order will be ready soon.
keyPhrases.note: The waiter says this to confirm that the order has been received and the food is being prepared.

connectedSpeech.slow: I would like a chicken sandwich.
connectedSpeech.note: 'Would' contracts to 'd' after 'I' in fast speech. 'I would like' becomes 'I'd like'. This is very common and natural in spoken English.

connectedSpeech.slow: Could I have some orange juice?
connectedSpeech.fast: Could I have some orange juice?
connectedSpeech.note: 'Could' and 'I' link together in fast speech so they sound like one word: 'could-I' becomes 'kʊdaɪ'. The 'd' connects directly to the vowel sound of 'I'.
'Are you' blends together to sound like 'are-ya' in natural speech. Also, 'to' reduces to a short 'tə' sound instead of a full 'too'.
The 'd' at the end of 'and' often disappears in fast speech. 'And' sounds more like 'an' or 'ən'. This is very normal in everyday conversation.
'Thank' and 'you' link together so the 'k' connects to the 'y' sound: 'thank-you' becomes 'θæŋkjuː' as one smooth unit.

sections.title: Audio Dialogue: Lunch at the Café

content.context: Sarah and Tom are having lunch at a small café. A friendly waiter comes to their table to take their order. Listen to how they use polite phrases to order food and drinks.
content.audioPrompt: Listen carefully to the following dialogue between the waiter, Sarah, and Tom at a café.

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.text: Good afternoon! Welcome to Sunny Café. Are you ready to order?
lines.translation: Selamat siang! Selamat datang di Sunny Café. Apakah Anda siap untuk memesan?

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.text: Yes, I think so. I would like a chicken sandwich, please.
lines.translation: Ya, saya rasa begitu. Saya ingin roti lapis ayam, tolong.

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.text: Great choice! And what would you like to drink?
lines.translation: Pilihan yang bagus! Dan apa yang ingin Anda minum?

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.text: Could I have some orange juice, please?
lines.translation: Bisakah saya mendapat jus jeruk, tolong?

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.text: Of course! One orange juice. And for you, sir?
lines.translation: Tentu saja! Satu jus jeruk. Dan untuk Anda, Pak?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: I'd like a salad, please. Do you have a tomato salad?
lines.translation: Saya ingin salad, tolong. Apakah Anda punya salad tomat?

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.text: Yes, we do! Our tomato salad is very popular. Would you like anything to drink?
lines.translation: Ya, kami punya! Salad tomat kami sangat populer. Apakah Anda ingin minum sesuatu?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Yes, could I have a coffee, please? With milk.
lines.translation: Ya, bisakah saya mendapat kopi, tolong? Dengan susu.

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.text: Perfect. So that is one chicken sandwich, one orange juice, one tomato salad, and one coffee with milk. Your order will be ready soon.
lines.translation: Sempurna. Jadi itu satu roti lapis ayam, satu jus jeruk, satu salad tomat, dan satu kopi dengan susu. Pesanan Anda akan segera siap.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Ordering Food & Drinks at a Restaurant

content.summary: In this writing lesson, you will learn how to write polite sentences to order food and drinks at a restaurant or café. You will practise two important polite forms: 'I would like' (or 'I'd like') and 'Could I have'. You will also learn to add 'please' to sound more polite. By the end, you can write short conversations between a customer and a waiter.

blueprintItems.title: Polite Ordering with 'I would like'
blueprintItems.formula: I would like + a/an/some + food or drink item (+ please).
blueprintItems.example: I would like a chicken sandwich, please.

blueprintItems.title: Polite Requesting with 'Could I have'
blueprintItems.formula: Could I have + a/an/some/the + item (+ please)?
blueprintItems.example: Could I have some water, please?

blueprintItems.title: Using Short Form 'I'd like'
blueprintItems.formula: I'd like + a/an/some + food or drink item (+ please).

blueprintItems.title: Asking for the Menu, Table, or Bill
blueprintItems.formula: Could I have + the menu / a table for (number) / the bill (+ please)?
blueprintItems.example: Could I have a table for two, please?

mechanicsRules.rule: Always start a sentence with a capital letter. Names of people and the word 'I' are always capitalised.
mechanicsRules.why: The word 'I' is always a capital letter in English. Every sentence begins with a capital letter too.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use a question mark (?) at the end of a question. Use a full stop (.) at the end of a statement.
mechanicsRules.badExample: Could I have some tea please.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: Could I have some tea, please?
mechanicsRules.why: Sentences that start with 'Could I have' are questions, so they need a question mark at the end.

mechanicsRules.rule: Put a comma before 'please' when it comes at the end of a sentence.
mechanicsRules.badExample: I would like a salad please.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: I would like a salad, please.
mechanicsRules.why: A comma before 'please' at the end of a sentence makes the sentence clearer and more polite.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use 'a' before words that start with a consonant sound and 'an' before words that start with a vowel sound.
mechanicsRules.badExample: I would like a orange juice.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: I would like an orange juice.
mechanicsRules.why: The word 'orange' starts with a vowel sound ('o'), so we use 'an' before it, not 'a'.

mechanicsChallenges.keyRule: Start with a capital 'C'. The word 'I' is always capitalised. This is a polite request in question form, so end with a question mark. Add a comma before 'please'.

guidedLabChallenges.instruction: Imagine you are at a restaurant. Write 3 to 5 sentences to order food and drinks. Use 'I would like' or 'I'd like' for at least one sentence. Use 'Could I have' for at least one sentence. Remember to add 'please' and use correct punctuation.
guidedLabChallenges.example: I'd like a table for two, please. Could I have the menu, please? I would like a chicken burger and some fries, please. Could I have a glass of lemonade, please? Thank you!
guidedLabChallenges.placeholder: Start writing your restaurant order here...

guidedLabChallenges.title: Challenge 2: Write a Short Café Dialogue
guidedLabChallenges.instruction: Write a short dialogue between a customer and a waiter at a café. The customer should order at least two items (one food and one drink). Use 'I would like', 'I'd like', or 'Could I have' in the customer's lines. The waiter can say things like 'Of course', 'Here you are', or 'Anything else?'. Write at least 6 lines of dialogue.
guidedLabChallenges.example:
Waiter: Good afternoon! What would you like?
Customer: I'd like a cup of coffee, please.
Waiter: Of course. Anything else?
Customer: Could I have a slice of chocolate cake, please?
Waiter: Sure! Here you are.
Customer: Thank you! Could I have the bill, please?
guidedLabChallenges.placeholder: Write your café dialogue here. Use 'Waiter:' and 'Customer:' to show who is speaking...

practicumQuestions.prompt: You arrive at a restaurant with a friend. Write one sentence to ask for a table for two people. Use 'Could I have' and remember to add 'please'.
practicumQuestions.criteria: The sentence must use 'Could I have a table for two, please?' or a very similar correct form. It must start with a capital letter, include a comma before 'please', and end with a question mark.
practicumQuestions.sampleGoodAnswer: Could I have a table for two, please?

practicumQuestions.prompt: You are ready to order at a café. Write two sentences: one to order a food item and one to order a drink. Use 'I would like' or 'I'd like' for one sentence and 'Could I have' for the other. Add 'please' to both sentences.
practicumQuestions.criteria: The answer must contain two sentences. One sentence must use 'I would like' or 'I'd like' and the other must use 'Could I have'. Both sentences must include 'please' with a comma before it. Correct capitalisation and punctuation are required. Food and drink items must be real and appropriate.
practicumQuestions.sampleGoodAnswer: I'd like a cheese sandwich, please. Could I have a glass of orange juice, please?

practicumQuestions.prompt: You have finished your meal at a restaurant. Write a short message (3 to 4 sentences). In your message: (1) say that the food was good, (2) ask for the bill, and (3) say thank you. Use polite language.
practicumQuestions.criteria: The answer must have 3 to 4 sentences. It must include a positive comment about the food (e.g., 'The food was very good'). It must include a polite request for the bill using 'Could I have the bill, please?' or 'I'd like the bill, please.' It must include a thank you. Correct capitalisation, commas, and punctuation marks are required.
practicumQuestions.sampleGoodAnswer: The food was very good. I really liked the pasta. Could I have the bill, please? Thank you very much!

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Ordering Food & Drinks at a Restaurant

content.summary: In this speaking lab, you will practise ordering food and drinks politely at a restaurant or café. You will learn how to say polite phrases like 'I would like...' and 'Could I have...?' with correct pronunciation, stress, and intonation. Good pronunciation helps the waiter understand your order clearly. We will focus on rising intonation for polite requests and correct word stress on key restaurant vocabulary.
content.audioGuidance: When you order food politely, your voice should go UP at the end of requests like 'Could I have some water, please?' This rising intonation sounds polite and friendly. For statements like 'I would like a sandwich,' your voice goes DOWN at the end. Practise saying 'would' softly — it sounds like /wʊd/, not /wuːld/. The word 'please' should always sound clear and warm. Speak slowly and clearly so the waiter can understand you.

pillars.name: Polite Request Intonation
pillars.target: Use rising intonation for polite questions and requests
pillars.explanation: When you ask 'Could I have a glass of water, please?' your voice should rise gently at the end. This makes your request sound polite and friendly. Falling intonation on a request can sound rude or like a command.

pillars.name: Word Stress in Food Vocabulary
pillars.target: Stress the correct syllable in common food and restaurant words
pillars.explanation: Words like 'sandwich' (SAND-wich), 'restaurant' (RES-tau-rant), and 'menu' (MEN-u) have stress on the first syllable. Saying the stress on the wrong syllable can confuse the listener. Practise these words with clear stress on the capitalised syllable.

pillars.name: Smooth Delivery of Set Phrases
pillars.target: Say polite ordering phrases fluently without long pauses
pillars.explanation: Phrases like 'I would like' and 'Could I have' are very common in restaurants. You should practise saying them smoothly as one unit, not word by word. For example, 'I would like' should flow together: /aɪ wʊd laɪk/. This makes you sound natural and confident.

pillars.name: Clear Articulation of Key Sounds
pillars.target: Pronounce difficult sounds like /ʊ/, /ð/, and /tʃ/ correctly
pillars.explanation: The word 'would' has the vowel /ʊ/ (like in 'good'). The word 'the' starts with /ð/ (tongue between your teeth). The word 'chicken' starts with /tʃ/ (like 'ch'). Practise these sounds carefully because they appear in many restaurant phrases.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: In 'menu,' the stress is on the first syllable: MEN-u. But in the phrase 'a la carte,' the stress shifts to the last syllable: a-la-CARTE. Notice how the rhythm changes when the word gets longer.

In 'water,' the stress is on the first syllable: WA-ter. In the compound word 'watermelon,' there are two stressed syllables: WA-ter-MEL-on. The primary stress shifts to 'WA' and a secondary stress falls on 'MEL.'
In 'order,' the stress is on the first syllable: OR-der. When we add the prefix 're-' to make 'reorder,' the stress stays on 'OR' but the word now has an unstressed syllable before it: re-OR-der.

In 'chicken,' the stress is on the first syllable: CHICK-en. In the phrase 'chicken sandwich,' both words keep their first-syllable stress: CHICK-en SAND-wich. Practise saying both stressed syllables clearly.

drills.targetText: I would like a chicken sandwich, please.
drills.phonetic: /aɪ wʊd laɪk ə ˈtʃɪkɪn ˈsænwɪtʃ pliːz/
drills.focus: Smooth delivery of 'I would like' as one phrase unit
drills.hint: Say 'I would like' quickly together, almost like one long word: 'I-would-like.' Do not pause between each word. The 'would' sounds like 'wud,' not 'woo-ld.'

drills.targetText: Could I have a glass of water, please?
drills.phonetic: /kʊd aɪ hæv ə ɡlɑːs əv ˈwɔːtər pliːz/
drills.focus: Rising intonation at the end of a polite request
drills.hint: Let your voice go UP on the word 'please' at the end. This rising tone makes your request sound polite. Start the sentence at a normal pitch and gently rise at the end.
For 'that's,' put your tongue lightly between your teeth for the 'th' sound /ð/. For 'thank,' use the same tongue position but with more air: /θ/. These are two different 'th' sounds.

drills.targetText: Could I have a table for two, please?
drills.phonetic: /kʊd aɪ hæv ə ˈteɪbəl fɔːr tuː pliːz/
drills.focus: Stress on 'table' and 'two' as key information words
drills.hint: The most important words are 'table' and 'two' — say them a little louder and clearer than the other words. The waiter needs to hear these words clearly.

drills.targetText: I would like the grilled fish and a salad, please.
drills.phonetic: /aɪ wʊd laɪk ðə ɡrɪld fɪʃ ənd ə ˈsæləd pliːz/
drills.focus: Pronunciation of 'grilled' and linking words together
drills.hint: The word 'grilled' has one syllable: /ɡrɪld/. Do not say 'grill-ed' with two syllables. Link 'grilled' and 'fish' together smoothly: 'grilled-fish.'
This is a yes/no question, so your voice should rise at the end on 'order.' Start at a normal pitch and let your voice go up on the last word.

roleplay.context: You are at Green Café for lunch. Mr. Khoirul is the waiter. He will welcome you, show you to your table, and take your order. Use polite phrases like 'I would like...' and 'Could I have...?' to order your food and drinks. Remember to say 'please' and 'thank you.'

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: Good afternoon! Welcome to Green Café. Do you have a reservation?
turns.translation: Selamat siang! Selamat datang di Green Café. Apakah Anda punya reservasi?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: No, but could I have a table for two, please?
turns.translation: Tidak, tapi bisakah saya mendapatkan meja untuk dua orang?

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: Certainly! Please follow me. Here is your table and the menu.
turns.translation: Tentu! Silakan ikuti saya. Ini meja Anda dan menunya.

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: Are you ready to order, or do you need a few more minutes?
turns.translation: Apakah Anda siap memesan, atau butuh beberapa menit lagi?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: I am ready. I would like a chicken sandwich and some water, please.
turns.translation: Saya sudah siap. Saya ingin sandwich ayam dan air putih.

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: Excellent choice! Would you like anything else?
turns.translation: Pilihan yang bagus! Apakah Anda ingin yang lain?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Could I have a cup of coffee after the meal, please?
turns.translation: Bisakah saya minta secangkir kopi setelah makan?

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: Of course! I will bring your coffee after your meal. Anything else?
turns.translation: Tentu saja! Saya akan membawakan kopi Anda setelah makan. Ada yang lain?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: No, that is all. Thank you!

practicumQuestions.instruction: Tell a short story about a time you went to a restaurant. Use the three story points below to guide your story. Speak in simple English sentences. Use phrases like 'I would like' and 'Could I have' in your story.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Now, please tell me a short story about a time you visited a restaurant. What happened? What did you order? Use the three points on your screen to help you. Speak slowly and clearly.
storyPoints: You arrived at the restaurant and asked for a table.
You looked at the menu and ordered your food and drinks politely.
You finished your meal and thanked the waiter.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I went to a restaurant. I asked for a table for two. I looked at the menu and I said, 'I would like a chicken sandwich and some water, please.' The food was delicious. I thanked the waiter and I was very happy.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ wɛnt tuː ə ˈrɛstrɒnt aɪ ɑːskt fɔːr ə ˈteɪbəl fɔːr tuː/
practicumQuestions.hint: Remember to use past tense for your story: 'I went,' 'I asked,' 'I ordered.' Use 'I would like' when you describe what you said to the waiter.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This storytelling exercise practises your ability to narrate a simple dining experience using polite ordering phrases. It tests your fluency, vocabulary, and ability to structure a short story with a beginning, middle, and end.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Tell a short story about ordering drinks at a café with a friend. Use the three story points below to help you. Speak clearly and use polite phrases.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Please tell me a story about visiting a café with a friend. What drinks did you order? How did you ask the waiter? Use the three points on your screen to help you.
storyPoints: You and your friend went to a café and sat down at a table.
You ordered drinks for both of you using polite phrases.
You enjoyed your drinks and talked with your friend.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Last weekend, I went to a café with my friend. We sat down at a small table. The waiter came and I said, 'Could I have two cups of coffee, please?' The coffee was very good. We talked and had a nice time.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /lɑːst ˈwiːkɛnd aɪ wɛnt tuː ə kæˈfeɪ wɪð maɪ frɛnd/
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'Could I have...' when you describe ordering the drinks. Remember to say 'please' at the end of your request. Speak at a comfortable pace.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This storytelling task helps you practise describing a social dining experience. You need to use polite request phrases naturally inside a story, which builds your confidence for real-life situations.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are at a pizza restaurant. Mr. Khoirul is the waiter. He will greet you and ask for your order. Order a pizza and a drink politely using 'I would like' or 'Could I have.'
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Welcome to Mario's Pizza! I am your waiter today. What would you like to eat and drink?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are sitting at a table in a pizza restaurant called Mario's Pizza. It is lunchtime. The waiter, Mr. Khoirul, comes to your table to take your order. You want to order a margherita pizza and a glass of orange juice.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: Mr. Khoirul is a friendly and patient waiter at Mario's Pizza. He speaks slowly and clearly. He will ask what you want to eat and drink, and he may suggest dessert.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I would like a margherita pizza and a glass of orange juice, please.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ wʊd laɪk ə mɑːrɡəˈriːtə ˈpiːtsə ənd ə ɡlɑːs əv ˈɒrɪndʒ dʒuːs pliːz/
practicumQuestions.hint: Start your order with 'I would like...' and end with 'please.' Say the name of the food and drink clearly.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay practises ordering specific food items in a restaurant setting. You need to use the polite phrase 'I would like' and name the items you want clearly.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are at a café. Mr. Khoirul is the barista. Ask for a hot drink and a piece of cake. Use 'Could I have' to make your request polite.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Hello! Welcome to Sunrise Café. What can I get for you today?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You walk into Sunrise Café on a cold morning. You want a hot chocolate and a slice of chocolate cake. Mr. Khoirul is the barista behind the counter. He is ready to take your order.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: Mr. Khoirul is a cheerful barista at Sunrise Café. He will greet you warmly and ask what you would like. He may ask if you want your drink to stay or to go.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Could I have a hot chocolate and a slice of chocolate cake, please?
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /kʊd aɪ hæv ə hɒt ˈtʃɒklət ənd ə slaɪs əv ˈtʃɒklət keɪk pliːz/
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'Could I have...' at the beginning. Connect your two items with 'and.' Do not forget to say 'please' at the end.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay focuses on using 'Could I have...?' to make polite requests at a café. Practise connecting two items in one sentence using 'and.'

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are at a restaurant with a friend. Mr. Khoirul is the waiter. Order food for both yourself and your friend. Use 'I would like' and 'Could we have.'
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Good evening! Welcome to The Garden Restaurant. Are you ready to order for both of you?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are at The Garden Restaurant for dinner with a friend. Your friend does not speak English well, so you need to order for both of you. You want grilled fish and your friend wants a beef burger. You both want iced tea.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: Mr. Khoirul is a polite and professional waiter at The Garden Restaurant. He will ask if you are ready to order and may ask about side dishes or drinks.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I would like the grilled fish, and my friend would like a beef burger. Could we have two iced teas, please?
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ wʊd laɪk ðə ɡrɪld fɪʃ ənd maɪ frɛnd wʊd laɪk ə biːf ˈbɜːɡər kʊd wiː hæv tuː aɪst tiːz pliːz/
practicumQuestions.hint: When ordering for someone else, say 'My friend would like...' When ordering for both of you, say 'Could we have...' Speak clearly and slowly.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay practises ordering for multiple people. You learn to use 'My friend would like...' and 'Could we have...' which are important phrases when dining with others.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are finishing your meal at a restaurant. Mr. Khoirul is the waiter. Ask for the bill and thank him. Also ask if you can pay by card.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: I hope you enjoyed your meal! Is there anything else I can help you with?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You have just finished a wonderful dinner at Green Café. You are full and happy. Now you need to ask for the bill. You want to pay by credit card. Mr. Khoirul comes to check on you.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: Mr. Khoirul is the friendly waiter at Green Café. He will ask if you enjoyed your meal and if you need anything else. He will bring the bill when you ask.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Could I have the bill, please? Can I pay by card?
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /kʊd aɪ hæv ðə bɪl pliːz kæn aɪ peɪ baɪ kɑːrd/
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'Could I have the bill, please?' to ask for the bill politely. Then ask 'Can I pay by card?' Keep your voice polite with rising intonation.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay covers an important part of dining out — paying the bill. You practise using 'Could I have...?' in a non-food context and learn useful phrases for finishing a meal at a restaurant.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the following restaurant vocabulary word clearly. Make sure you stress the correct syllable and pronounce each sound accurately.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Please say this word clearly: 'reservation.' A reservation is when you book a table at a restaurant before you go.
practicumQuestions.hint: This word has four syllables: re-zer-VAY-shun. The stress is on the third syllable: VAY. Say it slowly first, then try to say it at normal speed.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The word 'reservation' is important restaurant vocabulary. It has four syllables and the main stress falls on the third syllable: re-zer-VAY-shun. Many learners put the stress on the wrong syllable. Practise saying it with the stress on 'VAY.'

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the following sentence out loud. Pay attention to the correct grammar structure: 'I would like' followed by the item you want.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Please say this sentence: 'I would like a cup of tea and two pieces of toast, please.' Notice the grammar: 'I would like' plus the noun phrase.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I would like a cup of tea and two pieces of toast, please.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ wʊd laɪk ə kʌp əv tiː ənd tuː ˈpiːsɪz əv təʊst pliːz/
practicumQuestions.hint: The structure is: 'I would like' + a/an/some + food or drink + 'please.' Say 'would' as /wʊd/ — it is short and soft. Do not say 'I would liked' — there is no past tense here.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This drill practises the grammar pattern 'I would like + noun phrase.' The verb 'like' stays in the base form after 'would.' Also notice the countable noun phrases: 'a cup of tea' (singular) and 'two pieces of toast' (plural with a quantity word).

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say both words and notice how the stress shifts. First say 'dessert' (a sweet food after a meal), then say 'desert' (a dry, sandy place). The stress changes the meaning!
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Listen carefully. 'Dessert' means sweet food: de-SSERT. 'Desert' means a dry place: DES-ert. Now you say both words. Be careful with the stress!
practicumQuestions.hint: For 'dessert' (the sweet food), stress the SECOND syllable: de-SSERT. For 'desert' (the sandy place), stress the FIRST syllable: DES-ert. The double 's' in 'dessert' can help you remember — you always want MORE dessert, so it has more letters!
practicumQuestions.explanation: This stress drill shows how syllable stress can change meaning in English. 'Dessert' (de-SSERT, stress on second syllable) is the sweet course after a meal. 'Desert' (DES-ert, stress on first syllable) is a dry, sandy area. In a restaurant, you need to say 'de-SSERT' correctly so the waiter understands you want something sweet!

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the following two sentences. The first is a polite request (use RISING intonation at the end). The second is a statement (use FALLING intonation at the end). Feel the difference in your voice.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Say these two sentences. Number one, with rising intonation: 'Could I have the menu, please?' Your voice goes UP at the end. Number two, with falling intonation: 'I would like the chicken sandwich.' Your voice goes DOWN at the end. Now you try both!
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Could I have the menu, please? ↗ I would like the chicken sandwich. ↘
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /kʊd aɪ hæv ðə ˈmɛnjuː pliːz ↗/ /aɪ wʊd laɪk ðə ˈtʃɪkɪn ˈsænwɪtʃ ↘/
practicumQuestions.hint: For the question 'Could I have the menu, please?' — let your voice rise gently on 'please.' This sounds polite. For the statement 'I would like the chicken sandwich' — let your voice fall on 'sandwich.' This sounds confident and clear.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Rising intonation on polite requests like 'Could I have...?' makes you sound friendly and respectful. Falling intonation on statements like 'I would like...' shows you are sure about your choice. Using the correct intonation pattern is very important in restaurants because it affects how polite and confident you sound to the waiter.
